stem: The sentiments expressed by Washington in his Farewell Address most warn against partisan divisions that occurred before which of the following conflicts?
stimulus: “…Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally. “There is an opinion that parties in free countries are useful checks upon the administration of government, and serve to keep alive the spirit of liberty. This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796
options: The War of 1812
The Civil War
The Nullification Crisis of 1832
The Korean War
explanation: In the excerpt, Washington warns against the “baneful effects” of political parties. During the War of 1812, the War Hawks, largely Democratic-Republicans, saw war as an opportunity to grab new territories to the west and southwest. Their leaders were Henry Clay and John C. Calhoun. Federalists, on the other hand, opposed the war because it disrupted trade. Unaware that its end was coming, they met in Hartford, Connecticut, to consider a massive overhaul of the Constitution or, failing that, secession. When the war ended soon after the Hartford Convention, most people considered the Federalists to be traitors, and their national party soon dissolved. If you chose (B), you were close, but the Civil War involved more than just partisan divisions; it was fueled by geographical, economic, and ideological differences too. Choices (C), the Nullification Crisis of 1832, and (D), the Korean War, were not primarily partisan conflicts.

This within certain limits is probably true; and in governments of a monarchical cast patriotism may look with indulgence, if not with favor, upon the spirit of party. But in those of the popular character, in governments purely elective, it is a spirit not to be encouraged. From their natural tendency it is certain there will always be enough of that spirit for every salutary purpose; and there being constant danger of excess, the effort ought to be by force of public opinion to mitigate and assuage it. A fire not to be quenched, it demands a uniform vigilance to prevent its bursting into a flame, lest, instead of warming, it should consume.” Source: President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796
options: the popular election of representatives to the House
the indirect election of senators by state legislatures
the use of an electoral college to select a president
the nomination of judges to the Supreme Court by the executive branch
explanation: While all of these are features of the Constitution, you are looking specifically for things that, at the time, would have been believed to limit the influence of partisan politics. In the excerpt, Washington is expressing fear of public opinion becoming dangerous through political parties. Senators being indirectly elected, the use of an electoral college, and selection of judges by the president are all examples of the government not allowing people to directly control the government. Even though from the perspective of 2023, you may know that partisan politics plays into all of those things, at the time the Constitution was believed to limit party politics, except through popularly elected representatives. For that reason, (A) is the best answer.

As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816
options: The First Amendment, which guaranteed the right to free speech
The Tenth Amendment, which allows powers not granted to the federal government be granted to the states

The Twenty-first Amendment, which repealed the prohibition of alcohol
explanation: Although all of the Constitutional Amendments represent changes to the original document, the Twenty-first Amendment best exemplifies the sentiment in Jefferson’s quote. After only 15 years of banning alcohol, the Eighteenth Amendment (Prohibition) was repealed by the Twenty-first.

stem: Which of the following statements is most accurate regarding the existence of political parties in the early United States?
stimulus: “Some men look at constitutions with sanctimonious reverence, and deem them like the ark of the covenant, too sacred to be touched. They ascribe to the men of the preceding age a wisdom more than human, and suppose what they did to be beyond amendment…. But I know also, that laws and institutions must go hand in hand with the progress of the human mind. As that becomes more developed, more enlightened, as new discoveries are made, new truths disclosed, and manners and opinions change with the change of circumstances, institutions must advance also, and keep pace with the times.” Source: Thomas Jefferson, 1816
options: After the drafting of the Constitution, continued debates about states’ rights and competing economic interests led to the formation of political parties, such as the Federalists and the Democratic-Republicans.
Although Washington warned against the influence of political parties, he reluctantly accepted the endorsement of the Federalist Party.
Political parties did not exist until the War of 1812, when Federalists asserted control over foreign policies with France and Britain.
Two major political parties dominated early presidential elections until John Quincy Adams founded the Whig Party in 1824.
explanation: Correct: (A). In his Farewell Address Washington warned against political parties, and he remained officially nonpartisan — there was no formal Federalist Party endorsement for him to “reluctantly accept” in 1789/1792, when national parties had not yet formed. The first party system emerged in the 1790s out of post-Constitution debates: Hamilton’s economic program (national bank, assumption of state debts, protective tariffs) and disputes over states’ rights and strict vs. loose construction divided national leaders into Federalists and Democratic-Republicans. Choice (C) is wrong because the Federalist Party collapsed around 1815–1820, after the War of 1812. Choice (D) is wrong because the Whig Party formed in the 1830s in opposition to Andrew Jackson, not in 1824 under John Quincy Adams.

stem: Which of the following is a claim made by Jackson in the excerpt above?
stimulus: “Is there no danger to our liberty and independence in a bank that in its nature has so little to bind it to our country? The president of the bank has told us that most of the State banks exist by its forbearance. Should its influence become concentrated, as it may under the operation of such an act as this, in the hands of a self-elected directory whose interests are identified with those of the foreign stockholders, will there not be cause to tremble for the purity of our elections in peace and for the independence of our country in war? The federal government should remove its funds from the national bank and deposit them in state banks.
The national bank concentrates too much power in the hands of the bank’s executive.

explanation: While a few of these answers might be true statements, choose one that fits what Jackson actually says. Choice (D) uses familiar language from the passage but takes it out of context. Choice (C) provides the best summary of what Jackson says and is the correct answer.

stem: Supreme Court decisions concerning Native American tribes in 1831 and 1832 did which of the following?
stimulus: Map From 1830
options: reinforced the rights of states to remove Native Americans from disputed lands
denied them the right to sue in federal court but affirmed their rights to land that was traditionally theirs
voided previous treaties between Native American tribes and the United States on the grounds that the treaties were unfair
ruled that the federal government had a unilateral right to relocate Native Americans to lands west of the Mississippi
explanation: In the 1831 case Cherokee Nation v. Georgia, Chief Justice John Marshall ruled that Native American tribes were neither foreign nations nor states, and as such had no standing in federal court. In short, he ruled they had no right to sue. He argued further, however, that the tribes had a right to their lands and could not be forced to give them up by anyone, including the federal government. The 1832 case Worcester v. Georgia reaffirmed that position.

stem: The sentiment expressed by Beveridge best exemplifies which of the following?
stimulus: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898
options: Imperialism
Anti-imperialism
Isolationism
Manifest Destiny
explanation: In the excerpt, Beveridge is arguing that America is justified in ruling over less-developed nations with or without their consent but that those nations would surely appreciate the “just, human, civilizing” influence of the West. These sentiments are the hallmarks of Imperialism. Choice (D), Manifest Destiny, pertains more to domestic expansion, rather than international affairs.

options: Second-wave feminism

Republican Motherhood

The Adams family was not Jeffersonian Democrat or Libertarian, in the modern sense, so rule out (B) and (D), respectively.

Fearing the offensive violence perpetrated by the Branch Davidian cult, Attorney General Janet Reno sent troops to quell the subsequent standoff and later faced congressional criticism.

Choice (D) is tempting, but notice that Conyers says the Attorney General “offered” to resign. It does not say that she did. (In fact, she did not.)
